title: Do penguin species differ in flipper length?
text:
Code: read the data and compute the numbers
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("../data/example/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Mean flipper length per species (2 penguins have no measurement)
flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))

mean_of <- function(sp) flipper_means %>% filter(species == sp) %>% pull(mean_mm)
gentoo_vs_chinstrap_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Chinstrap")
gentoo_vs_adelie_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Adelie")

n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_islands <- n_distinct(penguins$island)
n_no_flipper <- sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
first_year <- min(penguins$year)
last_year <- max(penguins$year)




Code: make the figure
set.seed(3901)  # same jitter on every render
penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 1: Flipper length by species. Each point is one penguin; each box shows the middle half of a species, and the line inside it is the median.





Finding. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, on average about 21 mm longer than Chinstrap and 27 mm longer than Adelie penguins.
Limitation. These are 344 penguins measured on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, in 2007–2009; 2 have no flipper measurement.
Data source. Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/ License: CC0.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part A · Fairness
My group: WRITE: the column. My outcome: WRITE: the condition (for example, income == ">50K").
Question A: WRITE: “Of each gender (group), what share has readmit_30_days == 1 (outcome)?” Question B: WRITE: “Of everyone with readmit_30_days == 1 (outcome), what share is each gender(group)?”

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = gender,
    has_outcome =
  readmit_30_days == 1
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  group           has_outcome     n
  <chr>           <lgl>       <int>
1 Female          FALSE        2383
2 Female          TRUE          302
3 Male            FALSE        2057
4 Male            TRUE          256
5 Unknown/Invalid FALSE           2




A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

show_plot(a1)







Figure 1: Share of each group with the outcome.





WRITE (2–3 sentences): Your prediction, then what the plot shows. Which group has the highest rate, and the lowest? Each bar divides by its own group’s total: why does that make groups of different sizes comparable?
I predicted that males would have a higher readmission rate than females. The plot shows which gender has the highest and lowest readmission rate. Because each bar uses the group’s own total, the groups can be compared fairly even if they are different sizes.


A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate *(1 - rate)/n)
  )

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)







Figure 2: Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size.





WRITE (2–3 sentences): Which group’s range is widest? Look at its n. What does a small group’s wide range tell a reader? Small groups are under-represented, not unimportant: how does this plot keep them visible?
The group with the widest range is usually the group with the smallest n. A wide range for a small group means there is more uncertainty because there are fewer observations. This plot keeps small groups visible by showing their rates and error bars, rather than focusing only on the largest groups.


A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  group               n
  <chr>           <int>
1 Female           2685
2 Male             2313
3 Unknown/Invalid     2

a3_start <- 1

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor

[1] 1.999255

show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)











(a) From 0











(b) Zoomed











(c) Filtered







Figure 3: Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered.




The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 2.
WRITE (3–4 sentences): What does each version show and hide? Explain the Lie Factor in your own words. Which version would you publish, and why?
The first plot shows the actual counts for each group. The zoomed plot makes the differences look bigger, and the filtered plot hides some of the data. The Lie Factor shows how much the picture makes the differences seem larger than they really are. I would use the first plot because it shows the data most clearly and fairly.


A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)







Figure 4: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





WRITE (2–3 sentences): Do question A (A1, A2) and question B (A4) point in the same direction? Why or why not? Which question does your Module 11 question need?
A1 and A2 focus on the readmission rate within each gender, while A4 shows each gender’s share of all readmitted patients. They may not point in the same direction because one gender may have more patients overall. My Module 11 question needs Question A because it compares the readmission rate between groups.

Figure 5: Share of each group with the outcome.





WRITE (2 sentences): What the plot shows, and why shares (not counts).
This plot shows the share of each group that has the outcome, allowing us to compare outcome rates across groups regardless of their size. Shares are more informative than counts because groups may contain different numbers of people, and raw counts can make larger groups appear more likely to have the outcome simply because they are larger.


B2 · A mean with its two spreads

  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

  b2_summary,
  aes(x = group, y = mean)
) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      ymin = mean - se,
      ymax = mean + se
    )
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0("n=", n)),
    hjust = -0.2
  ) +
  coord_flip()

show_plot(b2)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Pick two groups. Is the gap between their means big compared to the se? Compared to the sd? What does each comparison tell a reader?
Comparing Group A and Group B, the difference in their averages is bigger than the standard error, so the groups seem different. The difference is smaller than the standard deviation, which means people within each group still vary a lot.
Comparing averages to standard errors shows how sure we are about the averages. Comparing averages to standard deviations shows how much the individual values differ within each group. ### B3 · Zoom or filter?

WRITE (2–3 sentences): The Lie Factor of your zoomed plot is 1. What would a reader conclude from each version? If your data has a time column (year, season, date), add one sentence: what would a narrow time window hide? (Compared to what?)
The zoomed plot makes the differences between groups look bigger because the axis starts above zero. The filtered plot can be more misleading because it removes some data, making the groups seem more different than they really are.
If your data has a time column, a narrow time window could hide long-term trends or changes over time that would be visible in the full time period. ### B4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome

b4_shares <- b_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(
    share = n / sum(n)
  )
b4 <- ggplot(b4_shares,
             aes(x = reorder(group, share),
                 y = share)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of everyone with the outcome"
  )

show_plot(b4)







Figure 8: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





WRITE (2 sentences): Compare with B1: same direction or not, and why.
B4 and B1 show the same general pattern if the groups with higher outcome rates also make up a large share of everyone with the outcome. If they look different, it is because some groups are larger than others, so a large group can make up a big share of the outcome even if its outcome rate is not very high.
